abstract: Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder, caused by prenatal alcohol exposure, remains a major public health concern, affecting up to 1 in 20 U.S. schoolchildren. As pregnancy is typically not recognized until five to six weeks of gestation, alcohol exposure often occurs unknowingly during the peri-conceptional period, a highly vulnerable developmental window of oocyte maturation, preimplantation and peri-implantaion. During this period, rapid cellular divisions precede lineage specification and organogenesis, rendering the conceptus sensitive to environmental insults such as alcohol. The placenta is increasingly recognized as an active mediator of alcohol-induced neurodevelopmental risk through the placenta-brain axis. We characterize peri-conceptional alcohol (PCA) exposure on placental development in a mouse PCA model mimicking human drinking patterns. Single-cell transcriptomic analyses on late gestation (embryonic day E17.5) placentas revealed disruption of extracellular matrix and collagen remodeling pathways within the labyrinth, processes essential for placental vascular development and mitochondrial dysfunction. Mitochondria isolated from E17.5 placentas showed compromised respiration and oxygen consumption. We assess placental vascular and hemodynamic functions with non-invasive dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI (DCE-MRI), enabling analysis across placental compartments for longitudinal evaluation of perfusion, substrate delivery, and contractile function. We demonstrate that PCA exposure arrests placental vascularization, perfusion, and morphological maturation, with PCA-exposed placentas at E17.5 resembling naïve placentas at E14.5. PCA exposure before implantation altered long-term placental programming, resulting in impaired placental perfusion and mitochondrial functions across gestation. These findings implicate placental dysfunction as a critical mechanism in Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder pathogenesis and identify extracellular matrix remodeling and mitochondria as potential therapeutic targets following PCA exposure.
